analysis.one_liner: Bans union contracts that require workers to pay union dues or fees as a job condition.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 88 Republican cosponsors and no Democrats, never received a hearing or vote in the House and died when that Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed federal labor law so that no union contract in any state could require a worker to join the union or pay dues or fees as a condition of employment, including at railroads and airlines. Today, some 28 states have such 'right-to-work' laws; this bill would have imposed one nationwide. Union membership and dues are how unions fund bargaining, and states with these laws tend to have lower union membership.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees in union workplaces who object to paying dues or fees would keep that money while still being covered by the union contract. Employers would also gain: unions with fewer dues-paying members have less money and bargaining power, which studies consistently associate with lower wage premiums in right-to-work states.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the parts of the National Labor Relations Act that let employers and unions agree to require employees to join a union as a condition of employment.
Strikes the Railway Labor Act provision allowing railroads and airlines to require union dues through payroll deduction under union security agreements.
Would apply nationwide, overriding state laws in the roughly half of states that currently allow union security agreements.

analysis.who_pays: Unions lose dues revenue and membership leverage; workers covered by union contracts lose collective bargaining power, since unions must represent every worker in the bargaining unit but could no longer count on all of them contributing. The historical pattern in right-to-work states is lower union density and lower wages for comparable work.

drawbacks.text: Federal law requires unions to represent all workers in a bargaining unit, not just members. A worker can quit paying dues yet keep the contract, grievance help, and negotiated raises the union wins — which shrinks union finances and, over time, bargaining strength.

States that adopted right-to-work laws have seen lower union membership and, in most economic studies, lower average wages for workers than comparable non-right-to-work states, so critics argue the bill would push all workers toward those outcomes.
Supporters of the bill argue compulsory dues infringe individual freedom of association, which is the bill's stated purpose of protecting the choice 'to refrain' from union activity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The individual benefit — a worker keeps some dues money — is real but small and immediate. The cost is broader and slower: unions must spend resources representing non-payers, bargaining power erodes, and the wage gains unions historically deliver shrink. On balance, the bill weakens the main institution workers use to negotiate pay and conditions, and its chief beneficiaries are employers who face weaker unions.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Joe Wilson of South Carolina introduced the National Right-to-Work Act on January 24, 2007.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor the day it was introduced.
On May 18, 2007, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, which was the last action it received in the 110th Congress.
The bill ended the Congress with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote of any kind.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers who keep union representation benefit, because a bill that would have weakened union dues and bargaining power nationwide never became law. Employers who would have gained leverage from weaker unions lost that opportunity for this Congress.

for.name: Rep. Joe Wilson
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House.

for.name: 88 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor listed was a Republican.

against.name: George Miller
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to and never scheduled a hearing or markup on it; the bill stayed at subcommittee referral until Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 88 cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill sat untouched in a committee chaired by a Democrat while Democrats held the House majority.

industries.note: The bill repeals the legal basis for union security agreements, cutting off dues from workers who choose not to pay while unions remain obligated to represent them. Dues fund the bargaining, contracts, and grievance representation that unionized workers depend on.

With fewer members paying dues, unions have less capacity to negotiate, giving employers more leverage over wages, benefits, and work rules — the mechanism behind the lower wage premiums found in right-to-work states.
